summary:
West Sulawesi stands under Indonesia's national framework. No source addressing West Sulawesi province directly was identified, so the province is assessed against the national position; a visitor to West Sulawesi should expect the legal and enforcement conditions that apply across Indonesia.

Consensual same-sex relations are effectively criminalised nationally. The penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment; because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, that provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations, and reporting indicates prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

Physical risk is rising. Vigilante mobs attacked transgender women across Indonesia in a wave on 14-16 July 2026, in which more than 15 trans women in Bogor were doused, stripped and beaten, with footage circulated online. Reporting in August 2026 ties the surge to hardened official hostility, including an executive order of October 2025 that lists the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture among non-military threats alongside terrorism, radicalism and drug addiction, placing LGBTQ+ people inside national defence policy.

Police raids on private LGBT gatherings continue. On 22 June 2025 officers raided a rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after reports of a 'gay party' and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International said the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside the national morality provisions. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and apply to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors; two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in Aceh in February 2025.

Expression is criminalised in ways a visitor can trigger. The 2006 Law Against Pornography and Pornoaction punishes any writing or audio-visual presentation showing or suggesting same-sex relations with up to seven years' imprisonment; the national broadcasting commission banned television and radio programmes presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal in March 2016, and the government has blocked websites and apps carrying gay or LGBTQ-related words, including Grindr. A bill to prohibit online content presenting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender behaviour was under discussion in 2025.

Custody has proved lethal for a trans traveller. In August 2022 Rodrigo Ventocilla, a Harvard student on honeymoon in Bali, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges and died in custody; his mother in Lima alleges police beat him and says authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release, and Indonesian police denied that violence was used.

Indonesia provides no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protections for LGBT people, and no national law protects people from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.
tangentialFactors:
Public hostility is measured and rising. A 2025 Pew Research Center figure put 93% of Indonesians calling homosexuality 'morally unacceptable', and a researcher documented markedly hardened anti-queer attitudes since 2016. Official posture matches: Indonesia voted against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2016, 2022 and 2025.

The enforcement texture a visitor meets in West Sulawesi is provincial as well as national. Aceh's caning regime and South Sumatra's morality provisions sit on top of national morality law, so conditions vary by province; Aceh is the only province where the religious-law penalties are documented as applied to foreign visitors present there.

No source addressing West Sulawesi province directly was identified, and no source documents enforcement, raids or vigilante attacks within West Sulawesi itself; the July 2026 mob attacks and the June 2025 villa raid are documented in Bogor and the Puncak area, West Java.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition in Indonesia requires sex reassignment surgery plus a judge's approval. Indonesia recognises only 'male' and 'female' sex descriptors on identity documents, with no third-gender or X option.

No national law protects residents from discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and Indonesia has no hate-crime protection covering LGBT people.

The 2022 penal code's extra-marital sex provision is the operative route to prosecution of consensual same-sex relations for residents, since marriage is unavailable to same-sex couples; reporting characterises prosecutions as selective rather than systematic.

Residents also face restrictions on expression and media: the 2006 pornography law, the March 2016 broadcasting ban on presenting LGBTQ behaviour as normal, government blocking of websites and apps carrying LGBTQ-related terms, and a 2025 bill to prohibit online content presenting LGBT behaviour that was still under discussion.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source addressing West Sulawesi province directly was identified. The province is assessed against Indonesia's national framework, and enforcement patterns, local regulation and any vigilante incidents specific to West Sulawesi remain unresolved and not sourced.

Sources disagree on the penalty for the 2022 penal code's extra-marital sex provision: the national framework states up to two years' imprisonment, while one inventory source states one year. The higher figure is carried here; the discrepancy is unresolved.

The current status of the 2025 bill on online content presenting LGBT behaviour is unresolved; it was under discussion as of 2025 and no source confirms enactment.

Whether the July 2026 mob attacks reached West Sulawesi is not sourced; the documented incidents are located in Bogor, West Java.
